title: Who it's really for
setting: A founder and a marketer narrow down an audience that is far too wide.

lines.t: Our target audience is small business owners.
In Bulgaria that's 300,000 people. Who is it really for?
Owners of firms with five to twenty staff who still do their own invoicing.
That's a niche, and now we can write to them.
Doesn't that limit us?
It makes you findable. What's their pain point?
Spending Sunday evening on paperwork.
Then there's your value proposition in one sentence: get your Sunday back.
And our unique selling point?
Nobody else here connects to the Bulgarian tax system. That's the positioning, and it's a fact rather than an adjective.
Where does brand voice come into it?

In how you say all of it. Do the market research first, follow one customer journey from advert to paid invoice, and write the way they talk at that desk on a Sunday. Brand awareness comes from being recognisable, and you can't be recognisable to everyone.

title: Why the ad failed
setting: Reviewing a campaign that got clicks but no leads.

lines.t: Fifty thousand impressions and four leads. What went wrong?
The click-through rate was fine. The landing page lost them.
What's on it?
Our history, our team, three paragraphs about quality.
And the call to action?
At the bottom. It says 'Learn more', which asks for nothing.
So the ad promised a solution and the page talked about us.
Exactly. I'd rewrite it around one pain point and one action.
Do that, and let's A/B test two headlines before we spend more.
Agreed. Same budget, two weeks, then we compare conversion rates.

title: Two hundred clicks, three sign-ups
setting: The advertising is working and the page behind it is not.

lines.t: The paid ads are working. Two hundred clicks last week.
And three sign-ups.
The click-through rate is up 40%.
So the advert is doing its job and the landing page is losing them.
That page has everything on it.
That's the problem. One page, one goal. What's the call to action?
'Learn more'.
'Learn more' asks for nothing. Try 'See your first invoice in two minutes'.
I'll run A/B testing on the two.
Do that, and measure the conversion rate rather than the clicks. Lead generation that stops at the click costs money and returns nothing.
Then I'll report the return on investment per sign-up, and we'll see which part of the sales funnel is broken.

title: Forty people left
setting: An email went out and part of the list went away.

lines.t: Forty people clicked unsubscribe after the last newsletter.
Out of how many?
Two thousand. The open rate was 19%.
That's survivable. What was in it?
Three product announcements.
There's your answer. They joined for a checklist and we sent them a press release.
The lead magnet was 'Ten invoice mistakes'.
Then keep writing about invoice mistakes. One useful thing, one link, once a fortnight.
And the announcements?
At the bottom, in one line. The forty who left did us a favour by being honest.

title: Planning the content calendar
setting: Two colleagues plan next month's posts.

lines.t: We need the content calendar for October by Friday.
How many posts a week are we doing now?
Three. Two useful, one behind the scenes.
The behind the scenes ones get the most engagement, by far.
Then let's make it two of those and one offer.
What about the lead magnet? It's been the same PDF since spring.
Good point. A fresh one would give us something to talk about.
I'll draft it. Something short, ten email templates maybe.
Perfect. That's evergreen content, we can use it all year.
I'll have a draft by Wednesday so you can review it.

title: The post that worked
setting: One post in March outperformed everything else, and nobody is sure why.

lines.t: One post did more than everything else in March.
The one about the invoice mistake?
Reach of 40,000, and the engagement was six times our average.
Impressions were higher still, because people came back to read the comments.
Why did that one go viral and the other eleven sink?
Because it was storytelling. A real client, a real number, and one sentence of copywriting at the top.
The headline was 'I lost 4,000 leva to a typo'.
That's a headline. Our tagline hasn't done that in three years.
Can we repeat it on demand?
Nobody can. But it's evergreen content, so it keeps pulling organic traffic every month.
Should we use an influencer to create buzz for the launch?
One who actually runs a small business. And skip the giveaway, or we'll collect two thousand emails from people who want a free mug.
Then it all goes in the content calendar and we stop guessing every Monday morning.

title: Before anyone else
setting: Planning a launch around the people who have already been waiting.

lines.t: The product launch is the 3rd of October.
Do a soft launch first, with the twenty people on the waiting list.
They've been waiting since June.
Which is why they'll forgive the rough edges. Give them an early bird price and ask for a testimonial after two weeks.
Do we still offer a free trial?
Fourteen days, and you call on day three. That one call decides customer retention for the year.
Our churn last year was 30%.
Most of it in month one, from people who never finished setting it up.
So the call is the fix.
The call, and one case study about somebody exactly like them. That's social proof they can check themselves.
And selling more to the ones who stay?
Upsell the bigger plan once they've outgrown the small one. Cross-sell the training to anyone who asks the same question twice.
Then the twenty on the list get a referral link, because they know other people with the same Sunday problem.
